findings.description: A task whose timeout or caller cancellation expires before `git worktree add` completes returns a `TaskResult` containing `worktree` and `log` paths even though neither artifact is guaranteed to exist. The log is created only after worktree creation succeeds, and the failed worktree creation output is stored only in `error`. This violates the failure-inspection requirement and makes the persisted artifact references misleading.
findings.reproduction: Execute a valid one-task plan with `Timeout: "1ns"` and an external new `OutputDir`. After Execute returns failure, inspect `result.Tasks[0].Worktree` and `result.Tasks[0].Log`: `runTaskCommand` observes the already-expired context before starting `git worktree add`, while `appendLog` is never reached, so both reported paths are absent. The same path is reachable when the caller context is cancelled during worktree setup.

findings.description: Every failure from the integration `git merge` is reported as an `integration conflict`, including context cancellation, timeout, hook failure, I/O failure, and invalid Git state. This makes cancellation and operational failures indistinguishable from actual content conflicts and is not truthful failure reporting.
findings.reproduction: Configure an external `pre-merge-commit` hook that blocks only when `$PWD` is the run's `integration` worktree. Run a one-task plan that creates a commit, wait until the integration hook starts, then cancel the Execute context. The merge is killed and returns `context canceled`, but Execute returns `workflow: integration conflict for task ...: context canceled` even though the task edits have no conflicting paths.

findings.description: On non-Unix targets such as Windows, cancellation kills only the direct task process. A task that launches descendants can therefore continue executing after the workflow has returned cancellation, contrary to the requirement that execution stops. The Unix implementation correctly uses a process group, but the fallback has no equivalent tree termination.
findings.reproduction: On Windows, run a command task whose parent process starts a child that waits briefly and writes a marker, then waits. Cancel the workflow after the child starts. `terminateTaskCommand` calls only `cmd.Process.Kill()`; after Execute returns failure, the child remains alive and writes the marker. The existing nested-process cancellation regression is Unix-build-tagged and therefore does not cover this path.
